question.text: Why did the first attempt at launching IRFs in India (June 2003) fail?

answer.text: Due to inadequate product design, lack of participation, and mismatch between the contract specifications and market needs
Because the RBI prohibited banks from trading
Due to a global financial crisis that affected all markets
Because the products were physically settled and delivery infrastructure was not available

explanation.text: The Logic: The June 2003 IRF launch covered a 91-day T-Bill future, a 6% 10-year notional bond future, and a zero-coupon 10-year GOI future, and was withdrawn soon after. The workbook attributes the failure to product-design drawbacks - cheapest-to-deliver complications, physical settlement, and the use of a zero-coupon yield curve - which made the contracts ill-suited to actual hedging. The Trap: RBI did not outright prohibit banks, the 2008 global crisis post-dated the 2003 launch, and the issue was not simply delivery infrastructure but the broader product-design choices around the underlying and settlement mechanics. Note: The 2013 redesign deliberately replaced these features with a single liquid GOI bond underlying and cash settlement, directly addressing the product-design drawbacks identified in 2003.
